newsitem.title: UK: UK electricity firms offer green power - at a price.
newsitem.headline: UK electricity firms offer green power - at a price.

text.p: Environmentally concerned electricity users in Britain are about to get the chance to put their money where their ethics are, and pay more for green power.

Premium-rate green energy packages will soon be offered to British consumers as a first step towards making electricity generated from renewable resources competitive with fossil fuels, industry sources said on Monday.
Customers will be asked to pay about 10 percent extra on bills to ensure their electricity is generated from wind, solar power, sewage or other renewable resources.
"It has to be deemed a premium product because supply is constrained," said Neil Humphries of South West Electricity Plc (SWEB), a leader in the green electricity market.
"But demand is encouraging and supplies should increase...and as the technology gets more mature the prices should come down," he added.
According to a national poll, two-thirds of British people would prefer renewable electricity, and one fifth said they would be willing to pay up to 15 percent more for it.
SWEB launched its "green electron" scheme on a pilot basis last year, supplying one of its biggest customers, Stroud District Council, with renewable power for nine months.
The company now hopes to extend the pilot to some small business customers and domestic users before opening it up to all customers in 1998.
Electricity cannot be stored, and so such schemes operate on a matching basis -- by estimating customers' demand and contracting the same amount of electricity from renewable generators.
"We give a 100 percent guarantee that the supply is from renewables," said Humphries.

The company described the Stroud pilot as "successful" after an audit was carried out by the World Wildlife Fund for Nature, but showing that competition is already hotting up in this young market, the Council switched to a cheaper renewable supplier after its nine-month trial ended.

SWEB was one of the first of the regional electricity companies to get involved in renewable generation with a windfarm in Cornwall, but it hopes to provide green electricity from a whole spectrum of technologies including landfill gas, chicken litter plants, solar power, and waste incineration.
Another company planning to offer its customers a green alternative is Eastern Electricity, a unit of Energy Group.
The company plans to launch a new green tariff in October, open first to domestic users and later to larger industrial customers.

Strong demand for this kind of energy means the new tariff will be an essential part of Eastern's strategy when the electricity market is opened to competition in 1998, said spokesman David Betteridge.
"No doubt there is a demand for it and this is part and parcel of going into competition," he said.

At present, just two percent of Britain's electricity supply comes from renewable sources, with more than half subsidised by the government's Non Fossil Fuel Obligation, a levy on fossil fuels introduced in 1990.

"Most renewable energy over last 10 to 15 years has come through this mechanism. The system needs to be kick-started to meet the targets of CO2 reduction the Government has set," said SWEB's Humphries.
But environmental lobby group Friends of the Earth believes that renewable energy could account for 50 percent of Britain's electricity by the middle of the next century.
The group claims that wind power is already competitive with coal-fired power stations and says that customers shouldn't have to pay extra for green supplies.

"Renewable energy has great potential in this country. Wind power is already competitive with coal-fired without a subsidy, but not quite with gas power," said Friends of the Earth energy campaigner Anna Stanford.
"We would dispute the need for a premium on renewables, in a few years they will be able to compete on their own," she added.
While onshore wind farms often draw criticism for blighting local landscapes, Stanford said that offshore windfarms have enormous potential as a new supply source.
Four offshore farms already exist around the world, including ones offshore Denmark and Germany, while another is planned for the North Sea off Norfolk in the east of England.
